FNAF
FNAF or F-N-A-F
proper noun / acronym (Gen Alpha slang)
Acronym for Five Nights at Freddy’s, a horror video game by the independent developer Scott Cawthon, released in August 2014. The player is a night guard at Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza who must survive five nights as the restaurant’s animatronic mascots — Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, Foxy — stalk him; the series’ lore reveals that the animatronics are possessed by the spirits of murdered children. Dozens of sequels, books, and spin-offs followed, and a Blumhouse film (October 2023) and its sequel (2025) made FNAF a Gen Alpha phenomenon from merch aisles to birthday cakes.

Biblical Definition

FNAF — Five Nights at Freddy’s — is the horror series about haunted animatronic animals in a pizza restaurant, and to Gen Alpha it is as familiar as cartoons once were: plush Freddys, FNAF birthday parties, endless lore videos about who killed whom. The Christian observation: underneath the jump-scares, FNAF’s story is about dead children whose souls are trapped in machines, wandering and seeking revenge. That is a sorrowful lie about death, and children deserve the truth. Scripture says that death is a single appointment, followed by God’s judgment, not a haunting: "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Heb 9:27). The dead do not wander between worlds; there is "a great gulf fixed" (Luk 16:26). And the little ones are not forgotten or trapped: Jesus said their "angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven" (Mat 18:10), and "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven" (Mat 19:14). A father can tell a five-year-old: "That’s a made-up story about sad ghosts. The true story is that Jesus loves children, and no child is ever lost to Him." And to an older child obsessed with the lore, he can ask: what does the story believe about death — and what does Jesus say?

Webster 1828 Definition

Acronym for Five Nights at Freddy’s (2014; films 2023 and 2025) — haunted-animatronic horror whose lore of trapped child-ghosts is answered by Scripture’s truth about death, judgment, and the children Jesus receives.

FNAF, proper n. / acronym (horror franchise, 2014–present; Gen Alpha usage) Five Nights at Freddy’s; the series, its characters, and its lore. "Can I have a FNAF party?"

Characters in kid lore: Freddy Fazbear, Bonnie, Chica, Foxy, Golden Freddy, Springtrap; the villain William Afton ("Purple Guy").

Decode for parents: the merch is cute; the story is about murdered children and vengeful ghosts.

Key Scripture

Heb 9:27 — "And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:"

Luk 16:26 — "And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence."

Mat 18:10 — "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven."

Mat 19:14 — "But Jesus said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven."

Modern Corruption

FNAF’s lore teaches that dead children haunt machines in sorrow and revenge; Scripture teaches one death, one judgment, and a Savior who receives the little ones.

expand to see more

Children are drawn to FNAF less for the scares than for the mystery — the lore of who died, who killed them, whose soul is in which suit. But the mystery carries a worldview: the dead wander, restless, trapped, bent on vengeance. That is pagan ghost-belief in a pizza restaurant, and children absorb it as a picture of what happens when people die.

Correct the worldview without mocking the child’s interest. Teach Hebrews 9:27 and Luke 16; teach that vengeance belongs to God (Rom 12:19), and that the children Jesus blesses are not trapped anywhere. If a child is grieving or frightened of death, FNAF is a poor teacher and the Gospel a good one: the grave is not haunted, it is defeated.
